one_liner: Zig CLI and MCP server that runs read-only SQL on raw CSV files, about 3x faster than DuckDB's raw-CSV path.
what_it_does: csvql is a single static binary that runs a SELECT-only SQL dialect directly on CSV/TSV files or stdin, with no ingest step. The dialect covers WHERE, GROUP BY/HAVING, ORDER BY/LIMIT/OFFSET, inner hash joins, non-correlated IN-subqueries and about 40 scalar and date functions. The query text looks like DuckDB's (FROM 'file.csv'), but there are no tables or persistent storage, no outer joins, UNION or window functions, and columns are untyped strings that are coerced when compared. It also runs as an MCP stdio server (csv_query, csv_schema, csv_list) for LLM agents, and has Python (pip csvql-query) and Node bindings over a C ABI that return the whole result as one JSON or CSV string.
how_it_is_fast: Files over 10 MB are mmap'd (MADV_SEQUENTIAL), split into newline-aligned chunks and scanned one chunk per core without locks; each worker keeps its own output buffer or GROUP BY hash map, switching to a shared Wyhash-sharded map after 50k groups. Record scanning uses Zig @Vector(16,u8) compares (SSE2/NEON) to find delimiters, quotes and newlines in one pass, falls back to a scalar quote-aware state machine only for quoted records, and returns fields as zero-copy slices into the mapping. ORDER BY uses pre-parsed f64 keys with an LSD radix sort, or a top-K heap under LIMIT. Much of the gap is fixed per-query cost csvql never pays (DuckDB's CSV sniffing, type inference and columnar materialization), which is why the lead is about 10x on a 417 MB file but about 3.2x on 8 GB, where the author measures csvql's COUNT(*) at 1.05 s against 1.92 s for cat over the same file.
when_to_use: One-off or occasional aggregates, filters and DISTINCT over a single large CSV, with low-to-moderate group counts, when DuckDB's ingest would not pay off (2.1 GB native store and about 26 s one-time load for the 8 GB taxi file).
Giving an LLM agent read-only query access to local CSVs, or remote ones over SSH, through MCP, sandboxed with --root and logged with --audit.

Joining a big CSV against small lookup CSVs (the right side is loaded into memory, the left is streamed and probed in parallel) when output order does not matter. The 2M x 6-row joins measured 29-89x faster than DuckDB on raw CSV.
Shell pipelines doing LIKE or WHERE filtering with CSV, JSON or JSONL output on multi-core Apple Silicon or x86-64. LIMIT without ORDER BY stops early.
Low-memory machines that must scan multi-GB CSVs without loading them. Peak footprint stayed around 30 MB on the 8 GB file for low-cardinality GROUP BY.
when_not_to_use: High-cardinality GROUP BY. The project's own issue #186 (open) measures 16.2 s vs DuckDB's 8.3 s (about 2x slower) at 5M groups over 75M rows, and that is after #184 brought it down from over 150 s.
Data you query repeatedly, or that needs Parquet, persistent tables or writes. DuckDB's ingested native store is faster after the one-time load, and csvql cannot write.
SQL beyond the subset: LEFT/RIGHT/FULL/CROSS joins, UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT, window functions, correlated or FROM-clause subqueries, and NULLS FIRST/LAST all return errors.
Full-table ORDER BY with no filter. ARCHITECTURE.md shows DuckDB 1.5x faster (0.108 s vs 0.163 s on 1M rows), because csvql must parse every row to extract the sort key.

Cases that need bit-reproducible floating-point results. SUM and AVG change in the last digits between --threads 1 and the parallel default (issue #185, open), so the parallel output also differs from DuckDB.

integration.form: Standalone CLI binary and MCP stdio server (Homebrew or prebuilt release). Also a C-ABI shared library inside the Python wheel (csvql-query) and the Node addon; the CSV reader can be imported as a Zig package.
integration.dependencies: None at runtime (build.zig.zon lists no dependencies). The correctness and benchmark scripts need a DuckDB CLI, and Python's query_df needs pandas.
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.15.x in practice. CI pins 0.15.2, and the source uses the 0.15-style unmanaged std.ArrayList API and the newer build.zig.zon format, so the README's 'Zig 0.13.0+' is out of date. The Python wheels need Python 3.10 or later.
integration.platforms: Prebuilt for macOS arm64/x86-64, Linux x86-64 and Windows x86-64; Python wheels add Linux aarch64. SIMD uses portable 16-byte @Vector code (SSE2/NEON), so AVX is not required. The differential tests against DuckDB run in CI only on Ubuntu x86-64 and macOS-14 arm64; Windows gets build and unit tests only.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for concurrent library calls. The CLI is multi-threaded internally (--threads N, 0 = auto). Each C-ABI call runs on its own thread with a 64 MB stack, uses libc malloc and shares no handle.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it accepts DuckDB-style SELECT text over CSV paths, but only a SELECT subset with INNER joins only, untyped columns, documented output differences (NULL written as an empty field, LENGTH counting bytes, fractional DATEDIFF, an empty field matching col = ''), and no tables or storage.

gotchas: Join output order, and GROUP BY output without ORDER BY, is undefined. Parallel SUM/AVG differ in the last digits from single-threaded runs and from DuckDB (issue #185).

Rows wider than the fixed 256-slot field buffer: several scan paths in engine.zig and parallel_mmap.zig catch TooManyColumns with 'continue', which silently skips the row, or truncate the row. The allocating parseCSVFields limit is 64 fields. None of this is documented, so very wide CSVs are unsafe.

Treat the memory numbers with care. BENCHMARKS.md's '1.8 MB vs 63.5 MB' predates parallel execution; the author's own 2026-08-17 audit measured about 53-74 MB max RSS. The taxi figures use macOS 'peak memory footprint', which leaves out clean mmap'd file pages and so favors csvql's design, and issue #186 notes that max RSS understates badly once macOS compresses pages.

Without --strict, a WHERE numeric comparison against a non-numeric cell silently drops that row. In SQL mode, SELECT * with no LIMIT streams the whole file (#170). The project has fixed a long list of silent wrong-answer bugs (#139 parallel aggregate undercount on large files, #142 and #154 dropped AND/OR branches), and correctness rests on differential testing against DuckDB.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick csvql over Apache DataFusion, or DuckDB itself, for a raw CSV you will query only a few times with scans, low-cardinality aggregates or lookup joins, especially as a small static binary or an agent's MCP tool; its own 1M-row taxi-sample run puts it about 1.9x ahead of DataFusion 52.1.0 with about 5.6x less memory. Pick DataFusion, Databend or chDB when you need full SQL, Parquet or table storage, outer joins, window functions or high-cardinality aggregation.
verified_claims_summary: First-party wall-clock times for whole CLI processes (startup included), best-of-N on a warm page cache, with csvql built -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (Zig version unstated) and DuckDB CLI 1.5.5 (read_csv_auto) both reading raw CSV without ingest: on the 20M-row, 8 GB NYC taxi CSV on an unnamed Apple M-series machine, csvql 2.6.0 ran the four Billion-Taxi-Rides GROUP BY queries in 1.39-1.52 s vs 4.61-4.71 s (3.1-3.4x). On a 2M-row, 56 MB synthetic file on an M2 Pro, aggregates took 12-56 ms vs 130-160 ms, a gap the author attributes mostly to DuckDB's startup and CSV-reader setup.
status_note: Actively developed with frequent releases (v2.7.0 on 2026-09-14), almost entirely by one author (276 of about 322 contributions). It is MIT-licensed and installable via Homebrew, prebuilt binaries or PyPI wheels, but it is young (created 2026-02), has 28 stars, and has no independent benchmarks or discussion (one Show HN post with no comments).
